verification_log.checks: Merck: uterine atony most common PPH cause; treat with fundal massage and uterotonics (oxytocin); fluids/volume. OpenStax: fundal massage for atony; oxytocin after placenta; hypovolemia signs

items.stem: A client who delivered the placenta 20 minutes ago has sudden heavy vaginal bleeding, a soft boggy fundus, tachycardia, and light-headedness. Complete the bowtie: priority condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Primary postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony
Stable, well-contracted fundus with scant lochia only

actions.text: Perform firm fundal massage and assist bladder emptying while notifying the obstetric provider
Administer ordered uterotonic therapy (e.g., oxytocin) and support ordered volume resuscitation
Discharge home immediately without assessment because early bleeding is always normal
Encourage unsupervised heavy exercise before evaluation
Withhold all assessment of the fundus and avoid notifying anyone

parameters.text: Fundal tone/height, lochia amount, and blood pressure/heart rate
Signs of hypovolemia (dizziness, pallor, ongoing bleeding) and response to massage/uterotonics

rationales.K1: Correct. Merck: uterine atony is the most common cause of PPH and is managed with fundal massage and uterotonics. OpenStax: early PPH is most often from atony with a soft boggy fundus.
rationales.K2: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not explain heavy postpartum bleeding and shock signs.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Findings show boggy fundus with heavy bleeding, not a well-contracted uterus.
rationales.A1: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: fundal massage stimulates contraction; a full bladder can impede tone.
rationales.A2: Correct. Merck lists uterotonics (e.g., oxytocin) and fluid resuscitation; OpenStax: oxytocin and fundal massage are first-line for atony.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Heavy bleeding with hypovolemia is an emergency.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Fundal assessment and rapid notification are required.
rationales.P1: Correct. Fundal tone and vital signs track ongoing hemorrhage (both sources).
rationales.P2: Correct. OpenStax lists hypovolemia signs; both sources emphasize response to massage/uterotonics.

items.stem: A nurse teaches caregivers of a 2-month-old about reducing sleep-related infant death risk. For each action, select Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Place the infant supine (on the back) for every sleep, including naps
Use a firm, flat, noninclined crib mattress with a fitted sheet only
Add pillows, loose blankets, and soft toys in the sleep area for comfort
Have the infant share an adult bed (bed-sharing) as the preferred sleep surface

rationales.R1: Indicated. Merck: back to sleep for every sleep; OpenStax: place infant on their back for all sleep.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Merck: firm, flat, noninclined sleep surface; OpenStax: firm, flat mattress with fitted sheet.
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Both sources: keep soft objects/loose bedding out of the sleep area.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Merck: bed sharing is not recommended; OpenStax: crib/bassinet in parents' room, not adult bed-sharing as the sleep surface.

items.stem: An older adult who cannot reposition independently is at high risk for pressure injury. Which nursing action best reduces sustained pressure over bony prominences?

options.text: Reposition the client at least every 2 hours (or more often if needed) using a written turning schedule and pressure-redistributing supports.
Leave the client in one position for an entire 12-hour shift to 'rest the skin'.
Drag the client across the sheets without lifting devices when moving.
Keep the head of the bed maximally elevated at all times without pressure reduction.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: patients confined to bed should be turned a minimum of every 2 hours; frequent repositioning is the most important pressure-reduction factor. OpenStax: repositioning about every two hours is the usual prevention rule for at-risk clients.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Pressure must not continue over bony surfaces for prolonged periods (Merck).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Merck warns against dragging because friction increases injury risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Merck: minimize head-of-bed elevation to reduce shear; pressure reduction still required.

items.stem: Complete the teaching for urgent nursing priorities in clinically significant hyperkalemia (ordered therapies).

ngn.template: Intravenous {B1} promotes cellular uptake of potassium. Oral or rectal {B2} promotes potassium excretion in the stool. Nurses also prioritize {B3} because hyperkalemia can cause lethal dysrhythmias.

B2.text: sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) or another potassium-binding resin as ordered

B3.text: continuous cardiac (telemetry) monitoring and ECG surveillance

rationales.B1a: Correct. Merck: IV insulin with glucose lowers serum potassium by shifting it into cells. OpenStax: IV insulin promotes cellular uptake of potassium.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) removes potassium via the GI tract/stool.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Unrelated to acute potassium removal.
rationales.B3a: Correct. OpenStax: continuous telemetry to detect lethal dysrhythmias; Merck emphasizes ECG changes guiding urgency.

items.stem: A toddler with acute gastroenteritis has mild-to-moderate dehydration, is alert, and can take fluids by mouth. Which initial rehydration approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Begin oral rehydration therapy with an oral rehydration salts (ORS) solution as recommended for mild-to-moderate dehydration.
Withhold all fluids for 24 hours to 'rest the gut'.
Give only undiluted fruit juice ad lib without an ORS plan.
Skip assessment and immediately start only intravenous fluids for every mild case.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: AAP and WHO recommend oral rehydration for mild and moderate dehydration. WHO: key treatment is rehydration with ORS.
rationales.C: Incorrect. WHO specifies ORS (clean water, salt, sugar mixture), not unrestricted juice as the rehydration standard.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Merck notes most children succeed with oral rehydration; WHO reserves IV fluids for severe dehydration or shock.

verification_log.checks: Merck: IV fluids first-line perfusion; prompt empiric antibiotics after cultures. OpenStax: cultures before antibiotics; timely broad-spectrum antibiotics; Surviving Sepsis bundle fluids/cultures/antibiotics

items.stem: A hospitalized adult meets sepsis criteria with hypotension concerning for septic shock. Which nursing/collaborative actions are indicated immediately? Select all that apply.

options.text: Establish/confirm large-bore IV access and begin ordered rapid crystalloid fluid resuscitation to restore perfusion.
Obtain blood cultures (and other ordered cultures) promptly, then give ordered broad-spectrum antibiotics without delay.
Monitor lactate/perfusion response and escalate for vasopressors if hypotension persists after fluids per protocol.
Delay all antibiotics for 24 hours to 'await a full week of culture results' before any therapy.
Discharge home without treatment because fever always resolves alone.
Ignore hypotension and withhold fluids intentionally.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: IV crystalloids are first-line to restore perfusion; OpenStax: fluid replacement is essential in septic shock.
rationales.B: Correct. Merck: collect cultures then give prompt empiric antibiotics; OpenStax: cultures before antibiotics and timely first dose are critical.
rationales.C: Correct. Merck monitors lactate and may need vasopressors; OpenStax Surviving Sepsis bundle includes lactate, cultures, antibiotics, volume, possible vasopressors.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Delaying antibiotics increases mortality (both sources emphasize prompt therapy).
rationales.E: Incorrect. Septic shock requires urgent treatment.
rationales.F: Incorrect. Fluids are first-line perfusion support.

Encourage only oral water without notifying the provider.
Discharge home for 'watchful waiting' despite shock signs.

items.stem: A trauma client develops sudden severe dyspnea, unilateral absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and progressive hypotension. Tension pneumothorax is suspected. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate immediately?

options.text: Prepare for immediate needle decompression (needle thoracostomy) of the affected pleural space while supporting airway/oxygenation.
Encourage deep coughing only and postpone any pleural decompression.
Apply bilateral tourniquets to the thighs as first-line therapy.
Discharge home without assessment because chest pain after trauma is always benign.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: immediate needle decompression for tension pneumothorax. OpenStax: tension pneumothorax is treated with immediate needle decompression.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Unrelated and harmful distraction from airway/chest emergency.
rationales.D: Incorrect. This is a life-threatening emergency.

items.stem: An adolescent with anorexia nervosa has severe malnutrition and will begin nutritional rehabilitation. Which nursing priority is most accurate?

options.text: Support slow, supervised refeeding with close monitoring for refeeding syndrome and cardiac complications; escalate for hospital-level care when medically unstable.
Encourage unsupervised binge eating of unlimited high-sugar foods in one sitting without monitoring.
Ignore vital signs and electrolytes during refeeding.
Advise complete permanent refusal of all nutrition.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: severe weight loss may require hospitalization and supervised nutritional supplementation. OpenStax: refeeding uses slow, measured intake with monitoring because refeeding syndrome can cause arrhythmias and death.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Rapid uncontrolled intake increases refeeding risk (OpenStax).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Electrolyte/cardiac monitoring is required (both sources).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nutritional restoration is essential treatment (Merck).

verification_log.checks: Merck: baby blues mild, typically 2–3 days up to 2 weeks; PPD lasts >2 weeks and is disabling. OpenStax: baby blues short-term (2–3 days), over by 2 weeks; PPD if symptoms do not resolve

items.stem: A nurse teaches a new parent about mood changes after birth. Which statement correctly distinguishes postpartum blues from postpartum depression?

options.text: Baby blues are relatively mild and usually resolve within about 2 weeks; postpartum depression lasts longer than 2 weeks and is disabling enough to interfere with daily functioning and infant care—seek prompt evaluation.
Any tearfulness on day 1 of life always equals lifelong psychosis with no treatment options.
Postpartum depression always ends in 24 hours without support.
Mood symptoms after birth should never be discussed with a clinician.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: blues last 2–3 days (up to 2 weeks) and are relatively mild; PPD lasts >2 weeks and is disabling. OpenStax: blues are short-term and should be over by 2 weeks; persistent symptoms indicate PPD needing care.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Overstates and mislabels transient blues.
rationales.C: Incorrect. PPD persists and needs treatment (both sources).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Both sources emphasize recognition and help-seeking.

verification_log.checks: AHRQ: check-back/repeat-back is closed-loop verification of exchanged information. OpenStax: teach-back has patient restate message in own words to confirm understanding

items.stem: After giving complex discharge instructions, which technique best verifies that the client understood the teaching?

options.text: Use a closed-loop check-back/teach-back: ask the client to repeat the key instructions in their own words and clarify any gaps.
Assume understanding if the client nods silently once, with no confirmation.
Speak only in unexplained jargon and leave immediately.
Refuse to answer any clarifying questions.

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ: check-back (repeat-back) is closed-loop communication to verify information was received; patients can use it for care instructions. OpenStax: teach-back has the patient restate the message in their own words to judge understanding.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Nodding alone does not confirm accurate understanding.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Barriers and unclear messages undermine teaching.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Clarification is part of effective communication (both sources).
